items.title: New research could lead to faster, trustworthy AI models for climate prediction
items.content:
Accurate, up-to-date climate projections are essential for planning decisions that enhance the resilience of power grids, protect public health, maximize agricultural yields, and more.

Now, MIT researchers have developed a technique that streamlines the production of fast, trustworthy, and adaptable artificial intelligence models for climate prediction.

These specialized AI models, known as climate emulators, can rapidly simulate the effects of human activities onto a future climate, predicting impacts on temperatures or sea level, for example.

Because emulators run in a matter of seconds, scientists use them to efficiently test thousands of varied climate scenarios. This provides more reliable estimates and can identify unexpected outcomes of regional interventions.

The MIT researchers developed a training technique that boosts the performance and adaptability of a climate emulator while using only a fraction of the data typically required. This significantly cuts production time for these practical scientific tools.

They show that an emulator trained with a much smaller amount of carefully selected synthetic data accurately predicts outcomes of scenarios it did not see during training, while traditional emulators failed to adapt to new situations.

“Climate emulators are especially well-suited for modeling policy-relevant scenarios. By using our method to generate optimized training data for an emulator, we can speed up the production of much more reliable emulators, so we can better trust their outputs for making policy decisions,” says Christoher Womack PhD ’26, who is now a postdoc at ETH Zurich and lead author of a [paper on this technique](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2620731123).

He is joined on the paper by Shahine Bouabid, a postdoc in the MIT Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); Andrei Sokolov, a research scientist in MIT’s Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3); Popat Salunke, a postdoc in CS3; Glenn Flierl, a professor of oceanography in EAPS; Sebastian D. Eastham, an associate professor at Imperial College London; and senior author Noelle E. Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and EAPS, and director of CS3. The research [appears this week](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2620731123) in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.*

**Speedier surrogates**

Climate scientists typically use earth system models (ESMs) to make long-term projections about how global temperature or precipitation could change in response to varying greenhouse gas emissions.

These enormous, physics-based models capture the major components and interactions of the earth’s climate in extreme detail. While powerful, ESMs can take months to run on a cluster of supercomputers — and that’s only to project one possible future climate scenario.

Selin and her collaborators design climate emulators, which are fast AI surrogate models that mimic the behavior of full-scale ESMs. Emulators help scientists test many scenarios, make more accurate forecasts, and explore specific pollutants and regional effects.

“Climate emulators can run in just a few seconds, so it really expands what we can do in terms of exploring these future climate scenarios,” Womack says.

When scientists design a climate emulator, they often train the AI model using a set of six to eight future scenarios based on realistic future trajectories of emissions. They must run each scenario through a full-scale ESM, making these datasets costly and time-consuming to generate.

The MIT researchers recently found that using realistic future scenarios as training data can lead to underperforming emulators that fail to predict unfamiliar or novel scenarios.

In this work, they developed an algorithm that generates a synthetic dataset of optimized climate scenarios tailored to boost one emulator’s predictive performance.

“Our algorithm might generate some weird scenarios which look nothing like a realistic future, but we don’t care so much if the training scenarios are realistic. We are just trying to make the best possible dataset to train an emulator,” Womack says.

Importantly, rather than needing to run a full ESM six or eight times to generate training data, a user would only need to run that model once.

**Tuning the training data**

The researchers begin by generating an arbitrary climate scenario using a fast and simple climate model. They test how well their emulator can reproduce the results of that ESM, which gives them a measure of error.

Because of the programming technique they used to build the training pipeline, they can iteratively update the training data to increase the emulator’s predictive skill. For instance, the algorithm could increase CO2 emissions dramatically in the year 2050 or rapidly decrease methane emissions in 2037.

Then the optimization updates the training data until the emulator’s error level reaches a certain threshold.

In the end, rather than resembling realistic scenarios in which emissions follow smooth trajectories, the synthetic data contain rapid variations.

“By introducing these high-frequency wiggles and oscillations, our data enable the emulator to extract a lot more information about the overall system,” Womack explains.

Their training algorithm outputs these emissions scenarios, which they can use to train an emulator that is more accurate and adaptable.

“In the future, we are definitely going to see climates and scenarios we haven’t seen before. If we can simulate these different scenarios more robustly, we can provide more reliable information to the stakeholders who need it,” Selin says.

For instance, an emulator trained with their technique can capture the effects of local pollutant control policies that reduce one pollutant while other emissions continue rising. The traditional emulators they evaluated failed this test.

In the long run, Womack hopes this work improves the usefulness of fast and adaptable climate emulators for policy formulation.

“This is such an important piece of the pipeline when it comes to creating useful tools that speak to stakeholder needs. Because the process of training an emulator can takes months or even years, the emulators we have are usually out-of-date. By cutting down that production time, I think this technique will be a game-changer in terms of getting updated tools into the hands of researchers and practitioners,” Selin adds.

In the future, the researchers want to test their technique using an emissions scenario generated by a full ESM. They also want to apply it to other types of climate models and explore its effectiveness in broader machine learning and computer vision applications.

This research was part of the Bringing Computation to the Climate Challenge (BC3) project and supported by Schmidt Sciences through the MIT Grand Challenges.

Sign Up to Our Free Weekly E-Brief

###### [Media Kit Download & Details](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/advertising.shtml)

News: [Suppliers](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news-suppliers.shtml)

**11 November 2026**

Aixtronâs revenue grow 60% in Q3, driven by opto demand for AI data centers

For third-quarter 2026, deposition equipment maker Aixtron SE of Herzogenrath, near Aachen, Germany has reported revenue of â¬183.6m (within the guided range of â¬180mÂ±â¬20m), up 60% on Q2’s â¬115.1m and up 54% on â¬119.6m a year ago, recovering further from the trough of â¬59m in Q1.

This reflects the ongoing ramp-up in optoelectronics business as well as the continued emergence from Q1’s trough in power electronics.

For the first nine months 2026, revenue was â¬358.1m, down 3% on â¬369.5m the prior year.
 After-sales contributed â¬87.8m (25% of revenue), up 10% year-on-year from â¬79.7m (22% a year ago.

Equipment revenue contributed â¬270.3m (75% of revenue), down 7% on â¬289.8m (78% of revenue)

Of the equipment revenue, optoelectronics accounted for 61%, gallium arsenide GaN and silicon carbide SiC power electronics for 19%, and LEDs & micro-LEDs for 18%.

Of total revenue by region, Asia fell year-on-year from 60% (â¬221.6m) to 54% (â¬193.9m), while the America rose from 23% (â¬83.3m) to 28% (â¬98.5m). Europe rose slightly from 17% (â¬64.6m) to 18% (â¬65.7m).

## Profitability boosted by favorable product and regional mix

Driven by the higher revenue and the better product mix and regional mix, quarterly gross margin has risen further, from 39% a year ago and 41% last quarter to 48% in Q3/2026.

Operating expenses were â¬30.6m, roughly level with â¬30.9m a year ago. This consisted mainly of R&D spending of â¬22.8m (albeit down from â¬23.7m a year ago).

Operating result (EBIT) was â¬56.7m (EBIT margin of 31% of revenue), up on just â¬14.7m last quarter and â¬15.4m (13% margin) a year ago, boosted by operating leverage due to the higher revenue volume.

Net profit was â¬35.4m (â¬0.31 per share), up almost doubling from â¬19.1m (â¬0.17 per share) last quarter and almost tripling from â¬13m (â¬0.11 per share) a year ago.

## Cash flow more than triples year-on-year

Operating cash flow was â¬138.4m, up from last quarter’s â¬119m and more than tripling from just â¬43.4m a year ago. This is driven mainly by higher customer pre-payments of â¬309m, up from just â¬44m at year-end 2025 (reflecting the strong order intake and backlog, the favourable composition of orders, and individually agreed payment terms), supporting the upcoming production ramp.

Free cash flow was â¬127.8m (up on â¬113.6m last quarter and more than tripling from just â¬39.2m a year ago).

As of end-September, cash and cash equivalents (including other current financial assets) were hence â¬944.8m (up from â¬816.2m at the end of Q2/2026 and â boosted by the placement in April of the firm’s inaugural convertible bond, of â¬450m â up from â¬224.6m at end-December 2025).

After deducting the liability component of the convertible bond of â¬353.9m, net financial assets amounted to â¬590.9m, up from â¬467m at the end of Q2 and â¬225m at year-end 2025.

The equity ratio has fallen further, from 88% at year-end 2025 and 61% at the end of Q2/2026 to 58% at the end of Q3, primarily reflecting the increase in total assets following issuance of the convertible bond.

“Our strong financial position provides us with the strategic flexibility to advance Aixtron’s development,” says chief financial officer Dr Christian Danninger. “It enables us to invest in our technology roadmap, strengthen our capabilities and further expand our position in attractive growth markets, creating sustainable long-term value.”

## Market & business development, order intake

Order intake was â¬274.9m, up 40% on â¬214.5m last quarter and more than doubling (up 122%) on â¬124m a year ago, driven predominantly by optoelectronics for AI data centers and, increasingly, also by power electronics. Of equipment orders:

- 68% was for optoelectronics applications (driven by laser applications in AI data-center communications), as demand for InP-based optical components continues to exceed original expectations and grow rapidly. The expansion of AI data-center networks remains the key structural driver for transceivers and InP in high-speed optical interconnects.
 Industry investment spans both 800G and 1.6T optical transceiver market: While 800G remains the established volume platform, the transition to 1.6T is expected to progress gradually as customer qualifications and supply chains mature.

- 24% was for power electronics applications, as momentum in GaN and SiC power electronics continued to improve in Q3. Initial orders for capacity expansions and a growing pipeline indicate the beginning of a recovery in power electronics, driven mainly by emerging low-voltage GaN applications for AI infrastructure power delivery (800V HVDC power) as well as industrial and AI-related high-voltage SiC applications. “Improving customer utilization, renewed order activity and preparations for new capacity provide increasing evidence of a recovery in GaN and SiC power electronics,” notes CEO Dr Felix Grawert. Broad market demand for GaN is expected to kick in once low-voltage adoption becomes broader. For SiC, customer utilization and consumables consumption is improving, and Aixtron has received the first new orders for 200mm capacity expansions.

“Together, these trends reinforce our expectation of a strong growth year in 2027, led by optoelectronics,” Grawert adds.

In contrast, LED/micro-LED system demand remains soft. However, AR and AI optical interconnect activity is increasing. So, the long-term opportunity remains attractive, reckons Aixtron.

## Order backlog rising despite production ramp

To serve all customers with shipments at their requested delivery dates, Aixtron is increasing manufacturing output at its own premises and in close cooperation with its suppliers. Output has risen each quarter throughout 2026 and is expected to increase further in Q4/2026.

Despite production continuing to ramp up during the year, equipment order backlog reached â¬549.4m, up on â¬456.9m at end-June and up 92% on â¬286.5m a year earlier (and more than doubling from â¬257.8m at year-end 2025).

Most of the order backlog consists of equipment for InP-based optical applications, providing revenue visibility well into 2027.

In addition to the strong order intake and order backlog, the composition of current orders and individually agreed payment terms also had a slightly positive impact on customer advance payments, (â¬197m, 43% of the equipment order backlog, in Q2). These advance payments contribute to financing the upcoming volume production ramp.

Inventories rose from â¬283.6m at end-2025 to â¬323.3m at end-Q3/2026, mainly reflecting higher levels of work in progress (WiP) for shipments scheduled in the coming quarters.

## Full-year 2026 guidance confirmed - strong outlook for 2027

Supported by the strong order backlog, in Q4/2026 Aixtron expects a further increase in output and revenue growth to about â¬200m.

For full-year 2026, Aixtron has hence confirmed its revenue guidance, which on 14 April was raised from â¬520mÂ±â¬30m to â¬560mÂ±â¬30m.

Of this, Q4/2026 revenue is expected to be up sequentially to â¬200mÂ±â¬30m (comprising â¬170mÂ±â¬30m from the equipment order backlog and â¬30m in after-sales revenue).

Aixtron also expects to achieve the raised guidance for gross margin of about 42% and for EBIT margin of 17â20%. This includes one-off expenses in the mid-single-digit-million Euro range related to the personnel reduction in operations in Q1 to create a more flexible operating structure after the very soft business outlook at the beginning of 2026 (this follows a prior 10% staff reduction between mid-2025 and mid-2026, from 1155 to 1035).

Based on the current sales pipeline, Aixtron expects to maintain or further grow the current strong order intake over the coming quarters, led by demand for optoelectronics and increasingly by growing momentum in power electronics. Significant growth is therefore expected in 2027.

Aixtron now expects capital expenditure of about â¬40m (rather than the prior â¬55m) for full-year 2026. This comprises baseline investments and about one-third of the announced â¬40m investment in the Malaysia expansion (rather than the previously forecasted two-thirds), with the remainder shifting to next year due to timing.

## Malaysia expansion progressing according to plan

Construction of Aixtron’s new manufacturing facility in Penang, Malaysia [a â¬40m investment in 2026â2027, announced in March], remains fully on schedule. The ground work and piling have been completed, the ground floor is almost finished, and Aixtron expects to be able to use the building from fall 2027 onwards, for first system shipments by end-2027. Located in a leading semiconductor ecosystem, the site will add manufacturing flexibility (expanding Aixtron’s manufacturing capacity by 25â30% by 2028), strengthen supply-chain resilience, support future growth and enhance long-term cost competitiveness, it is expected.

**11 November 2026**

JX and OXIDE enter into capital and business alliance agreement

Tokyo-based JX Advanced Metals Corp and OXIDE Corp of Yamanashi, Japan (which specializes in optical crystals and frequency-conversion technology) have entered into a capital and business alliance agreement. JX plans to subscribe for shares to be issued by OXIDE through a third-party allotment and acquire shares representing 7.66% of OXIDE’s total issued shares. The investment is expected to amount to about Â¥2.75bn, and JX’s ownership ratio is expected to be 7.12%.

JX operates globally, primarily developing, manufacturing and selling advanced materials made from copper and rare metals. The firm has positioned crystal materials as one of the pillars of its next-generation businesses. In response to the expansion of AI data centers and the growing use of optical communications within data centers, JX is investing up to Â¥150bn over four years to expand production capacity for indium phosphide (InP) substrates. To further grow its crystal materials business, it is also pursuing developing and commercializing new materials and technologies through co-creation with external partners.

OXIDE operates in the photonics field, with optical single crystals and laser-related technologies as its core technologies. In addition to offering optical materials such as bismuth-substituted rare-earth iron garnet (Bi:RIG, used in optical isolators), OXIDE is also developing next-generation optical materials such as thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) and expanding its business into quantum-related fields, including quantum communications and quantum computing.

Through the alliance, the two companies will combine JX’s materials development and mass-production technologies cultivated through its crystal materials business including InP substrates, its thin-film materials technologies and its global customer base with OXIDE’s optical single-crystal growth technologies, wavelength-conversion technologies, and optical-device and laser technologies. The companies will hence complement each other’s materials and technology portfolios.

Specifically, they aim to mutually leverage their expertise in mass-production technologies and manufacturing processes for crystal materials to further advance production technologies and mass-production capabilities, while also utilizing JX’s global customer base to expand their business reach. Furthermore, by drawing on their respective technologies and expertise in crystal materials, optical devices and lasers, the companies will work to create medium- to long-term business opportunities in fields such as optical communications and photonics-electronics convergence, semiconductors, and healthcare. They also aim to create new materials, products and businesses in quantum-related fields, including quantum communications and quantum computing.

Through the investment, the firms expect to strengthen their collaboration and accelerate technology development and commercialization by leveraging their respective strengths, hence expanding their business portfolios and achieving sustainable growth in the crystal materials and photonics fields.

items.title: Visteon, SHINRY and Infineon collaborate on single-stage onboard charger with GaN BDS technology
items.content:
[](https://www.appliedenergysystems.com/stakes)

Sign Up to Our Free Weekly E-Brief

###### [Media Kit Download & Details](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/advertising.shtml)

News: [Microelectronics](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news-micro.shtml)

**11 November 2026**

Visteon, SHINRY and Infineon collaborate on single-stage onboard charger with GaN BDS technology

Visteon Corp of Van Buren Township, MI, USA and SHINRY Technologies Co Ltd of Shenzhen, China, through their joint venture VisteonâShinry Power Electronics LLC (VSPE), are collaborating with Infineon Technologies AG of Munich, Germany to develop a single-stage onboard charger (OBC) for electric vehicles. Designed to deliver high efficiency and reliability while reducing system size, complexity and cost compared to traditional designs, the solution combines VSPE’s advanced converter hardware topology, proprietary control strategy and system integration expertise with Infineon’s gallium nitride (GaN) monolithic bidirectional switches (BDS). The companies announced their collaboration during the electronica 2026 trade fair in Munich.Â

VSPE’s single-stage architecture combines power conversion functions traditionally handled by separate stages and eliminates the bulk capacitors found in conventional two-stage OBCs. The approach improves reliability, reduces system complexity, enables more compact packaging, and lowers cost. The onboard charger supports both 22kW three-phase and 19.2kW single-phase AC charging, with full vehicle-to-everything (V2X) bidirectional capability, enabling grid interaction and greater energy flexibility.

Infineon says that its GaN BDS technology is particularly suited to the requirements of the single-stage architecture. Unlike conventional power switches, the monolithic devices integrate bidirectional voltage blocking and current conduction into a single device, allowing bidirectional switching functions to be implemented with fewer semiconductor components, simplifying the power stage. GaN’s high-frequency switching capabilities also help to increase power density and reduce the size of magnetic components.

“This collaboration brings together complementary strengths in vehicle electronics, power conversion and advanced semiconductors,” says Zilai Zhao, co-general manager at VisteonâShinry Power Electronics. “By combining Visteon’s system expertise and Infineon’s GaN leadership, we’re delivering a transformative solution for next-generation EV platforms,” he adds.

“Integrating Infineon’s GaN switches with our proprietary single-stage topology is a game-changer for power density and system cost,” claims SHINRY’s chief technology officer Mark Sun. “Our R&D team is fully committed to validating this innovative architecture to meet the rigorous reliability standards of global automotive customers,” he adds.

“Together with VisteonâShinry Power Electronics we are pushing the boundaries of onboard charging for the next generation of electric vehicles,” claims Benoit Rousseau, VP, GaN Automotive at Infineon. “Our GaN bidirectional switch, recognized as a ‘Global New Energy Vehicle Innovative Technology’ at the 2026 World New Energy Vehicle Congress, combines leading-edge switching performance and efficiency with a new level of semiconductor integration, enabling new power conversion architectures.”

**11 November 2026**

**WT to distribute Siversâ InP lasers and wireless solutions**

Sivers Semiconductors AB of Kista, Sweden (which supplies RF beam-former ICs and lasers for AI data-center, SATCOM, defense and telecom applications) has announced a global distribution agreement with electronics and semiconductors distributor WT Microelectronics Co Ltd.

With a 15% global market share, WT will serve as a global distribution partner for Sivers’ indium phosphide (InP) lasers and wireless beamformer products and solutions, connecting its product portfolio and availability at scale with customers globally. The agreement supports Sivers’ efforts to expand its commercial reach in markets where demand for optical technologies and high-capacity wireless connectivity continues to grow.

“Partnering with WT Microelectronics and becoming their first laser line-card gives Sivers access to an established global distribution network, strong demand creation capabilities and the ability to support production ramp fulfilments at scale,” says Sivers’ CEO Vickram Vathulya. “The WT partnership commitment is an indication of the strength of the innovation and scale Sivers is bringing to the ecosystems in AI infrastructure, SATCOM and defense.”

Yole Group forecasts that the market for InP continuous-wave distributed feedback (DFB) lasers for AI photonics applications will grow at 63% annually to $43.5bn by 2031. Among the applications for mmWave beam-former ICs, the LEO (low earth orbit) SATCOM market is a fast-growing segment, where Yole expects growth up to $1.2bn by 2031.

Sivers’ CW lasers and wireless beamformer technologies “address important and expanding markets, including AI data-center connectivity, satellite communications, and next-generation wireless,” comments Joseph Cheng, WT’s senior VP of marketing. “Our global distribution network and established customer relationships position us to bring these technologies to customers seeking advanced connectivity solutions.”

items.title: Nexperia expands SiC portfolio with 750V trench MOSFETs for high-efficiency power conversion
items.content:
[](https://www.appliedenergysystems.com/stakes)

Sign Up to Our Free Weekly E-Brief

###### [Media Kit Download & Details](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/advertising.shtml)

News: [Microelectronics](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news-micro.shtml)

**11 November 2026**

Nexperia expands SiC portfolio with 750V trench MOSFETs for high-efficiency power conversion

Discrete device designer and manufacturer Nexperia B.V. of Nijmegen, the Netherlands (which operates wafer fabs in Hamburg, Germany, and Hazel Grove Manchester, UK) has launched a new family of 750V silicon carbide (SiC) trench MOSFETs, combining low switching losses, temperature-stable RDS(on) characteristics and robust switching performance in a broad range of package options, including the introduction of TOLL packaging to Nexperia’s SiC MOSFET portfolio. Designed for demanding industrial and automotive applications, the devices enable efficient, reliable and compact power conversion systems.

As demand for more efficient power conversion continues to grow across sectors such as renewable energy, industrial automation, AI data centres and electrified transportation, designers must achieve higher levels of efficiency, power density, thermal performance and system cost. Addressing these requirements calls for power devices that deliver consistent, predictable performance across a wide range of operating conditions.

The new SiC MOSFET family is designed to help engineers address these challenges. Extending the company’s portfolio into the 750V voltage class, these devices are optimized for EV charging infrastructure, photovoltaic inverters, industrial drives, AI and high-performance computing power supplies, as well as onboard chargers, DCâDC converters and auxiliary drives applications. The additional voltage headroom supports robust operation under transient conditions while helping designers maximise overall system performance.

The devices combine low conduction and switching losses with excellent RDS(on) stability across their operating temperature range, helping to maintain predictable performance in real-world applications. Fast switching speeds, temperature-stable turn-off behaviour and a robust intrinsic body diode further support reliable operation in demanding hard-switching topologies. These characteristics can help to reduce cooling requirements and support higher system efficiency, particularly under medium and high load conditions.

A key addition to Nexperia’s SiC MOSFET portfolio is the availability of TOLL packages. As one of the most widely adopted surface-mount packages for high-power applications, TOLL combines a compact footprint with low package inductance, making it well suited to designs that require high power density and efficient high-frequency switching. The package complements Nexperia’s existing through-hole, bottom-cooled and top-cooled options, giving designers greater choice when balancing thermal, layout and manufacturing requirements.

“The introduction of our 750V SiC MOSFET family represents an important step in expanding Nexperia’s wide bandgap portfolio,” says Gaetano Pignataro, head of the SiC & IGBT Product Group. “By combining low switching losses, temperature-stable performance and flexible packaging options, including TOLL, these devices help customers increase power density, improve efficiency and simplify thermal management in next-generation power conversion systems,” he adds. “We are committed to providing engineers with the technologies they need to meet the growing demands of electrification, renewable energy and AI-driven infrastructure.”

The 750V family is available now in both industrial and AEC-Q101-qualified automotive variants, providing a scalable SiC technology platform for a wide range of power conversion applications. This enables customers to leverage the performance benefits of a common SiC technology across multiple system topologies while addressing diverse qualification requirements.

items.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
items.content:
Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.

The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.

## You had one job

Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/grok-build-coding-agent-leaks-oodles-of-confidential-info-some-belonging-to-spacexsi/)

items.title: MIT-led team receives funding to develop next-generation alternatives to modern weed killers
items.content:
MIT researchers will lead an up to $53 million effort, awarded by the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) as part of its STREAM (Systems for Tracking and Resilience in Efficient Agricultural-input Management) program, to develop next-generation weed killers that help farmers and protect human health.

More than 1 billion pounds of herbicide are used in the United States every year. Herbicides help farmers by preventing significant crop loss due to weeds, and they enable regenerative farming practices that protect the soil, but some weeds are becoming resistant to the most common herbicides.

Exposure to herbicides may contribute to increased risk of cancer, metabolic and endocrine disorders, and other adverse health outcomes. Farm workers can be exposed from frequent herbicide use, but many U.S. residents are also exposed to these chemicals in small amounts through food and drinking water.

The MIT-led research team will develop new generative artificial intelligence tools to help them discover herbicide alternatives that are more effective and developed with human health in mind. Such alternatives could also help to reduce U.S. dependency on imported phosphorus, which is a critical ingredient in a major herbicide, glyphosate.

“With herbicides like glyphosate and atrazine, there’s a real crisis because of resistance mutations that are coming,” says Christopher Voigt, head of MIT’s Department of Biological Engineering. “And if you combine the resistance mutations with issues around national security of the supply chain of the precursors to herbicides, we could find ourselves without these core agrochemicals that are absolutely essential for getting the high crop yields and economical prices that the United States now sees.”

Voigt is the principal investigator for the project, known as Precision Learning for On-target Weed control (PLOW). The team is also expected to include researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the University of Tennessee at Knoxville, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and Robigo.

The researchers are grouped into three teams that will tackle different aspects of the project, aligned with the STREAM Technical Areas. The generative AI group will develop models that can predict molecules — either chemical compounds or small interfering RNA (siRNA) — that disrupt the same plant enzymes targeted by glyphosate and other herbicides.

Glyphosate kills weeds by interfering with an enzyme called EPSP synthase, which plants need to produce several critical amino acids. After many years of herbicide use, some weeds have begun to acquire genetic mutations that allow them to become resistant to those herbicides, which makes them less effective and poses a significant threat to crop yields.

“There’s a real need for new herbicides because of resistance mutations that have been arising,” Voigt says. “There are also concerns about herbicides’ possible impacts on the environment and on humans, so it’s important to identify alternative ways of making herbicides, which as a general class of molecule are really critical to agriculture.”

The MIT-led team plans to design generative AI models that will be able to predict molecules that can help prevent resistance from arising. The models will also optimize for other features such as low cost of synthesis, low risk of inducing resistance, and low risk of harming humans or causing ecological damage.

The group developing these AI models is led by Connor Coley, the Warren K. Lewis Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering at MIT; Regina Barzilay, the School of Engineering Distinguished Professor for AI and Health at MIT; and Alexander Tropsha, the K.H. Lee Distinguished Professor in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy.

The models are expected to generate billions of possible candidates, which will then be tested by a second research team. This high-throughput screening group will be led by Angela Koehler, the Charles W. and Jennifer C. Johnson Professor of Biological Engineering at MIT, and Jaime Cheah, the associate director of scientific outreach and collaborative screening in the Center for the Development of Therapeutics at the Broad Institute.

“Those libraries will be screened both to identify those molecules that hit their target, but also to then provide all of that screening data back to the computational approach in order to improve it,” Voigt says.

Once the candidate pools are narrowed down, researchers on a third team will begin greenhouse studies to evaluate how each molecule performs under different agricultural conditions. That team will be led by Neal Stewart and Scott Lenaghan, co-directors of the Center for Agricultural Synthetic Biology at UTK; Patrick Tranel, the Tom and Peggy Ainsworth Professor of Crop Sciences at the University of Illinois; Tim Willson, the Harold Kohn Distinguished Professor at the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy; and Andee Wallace PhD ’20, CEO and founder of Robigo.

The first greenhouse tests of initial RNAi candidates are expected to be complete by the end of the first year of the program.

As part of this project, the research team will also develop living microbial systems that degrade agrochemicals before they reach food, soil, or waterways. Engineered bacteria, fungi, and srRNA will convert chemicals and formulation ingredients into biomass, providing a scalable strategy to reduce environmental and human exposure.

This research is funded by the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) under agreement number 140D042690030. The views and conclusions contained in this article are those of the authors and should not be interpreted as representing the official policies, either expressed or implied, of the United States government.

items.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
items.content:
Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting.

The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole [became publicly known](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/vulnerability-allows-attackers-to-log-into-some-linux-devices-sans-password/) last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.

## Attackers conducting "mature intrusions"

Security firm Greynoise [said Monday](https://sshole.events.greynoise.io) that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/vulnerability-that-lets-hackers-ssh-into-linux-devices-is-under-active-exploitation/)

items.title: The Race to Build a “Find My” for AI Chips
items.content:
In a bid to limit China’s AI capabilities, the United States imposed [restrictions](https://spectrum.ieee.org/chip-ban) in 2022 on the export of certain advanced chips to China. But throughout the AI boom those chips have kept [turning up in China anyway](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/smugglers-get-expensive-memory-chips-china-south-korea?rc=lgnx6w).

On 1 October 2026, the U.S. [arrested](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/california-man-arrested-smuggling-more-300-million-export-controlled-computer-servers-china) a man on charges of sending over US $300 million worth of GPU-equipped servers to China using paperwork intended for shipments to Malaysia and [Singapore](https://www.thewirechina.com/2026/11/01/u-s-export-controls-fuel-the-rise-of-asian-data-centers-serving-chinese-ai/). As chip smuggling and diversion continues, the United States is learning that the more it tries to limit the motion of its AI chips, the [harder they are to precisely locate](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/data-centers/illegal-nvidia-blackwell-ultra-b300-gpus-found-inside-state-owned-china-telecoms-network-nvidia-says-chip-smuggling-a-drop-in-the-bucket-insists-smuggling-remains-a-nonfactor).

To help curb the issue, the U.S. is turning to location verification. Last March, the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee passed a [bill](https://chinaselectcommittee.house.gov/media/press-releases/house-committee-passes-chip-security-act) requiring location verification for advanced AI chips. Ahead of the U.S.-China summit in late September, legislators [called](https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/09/schumer-presses-thune-for-vote-on-chip-export-bills-01089760) for a floor vote on that and related bills.

If such a requirement were to pass, how would chipmakers comply? They could build tamper-proof root-of-trust hardware, implement cryptographic signing and transmission, or possibly even fingerprint individual chips. These strategies could function as a way to keep track of where AI chips actually are in the world, much like how the popular [“Find My” feature](https://www.apple.com/icloud/find-my/) can locate misplaced Apple devices.

## Pings that pinpoint positions

Location verification can take different forms, such as geolocation mechanisms, inventory-management tools, mail-in inspections, and video inspections. A combination of approaches, such as ping-based location verification (PLV) supplemented by physical inspections, would be a feasible and robust approach, say the authors of a September [Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET)](https://cset.georgetown.edu/) [report](https://cset.georgetown.edu/publication/tracking-ai-chips/) on chip-location tracking.

To deduce an AI chip’s location, PLV measures the time it takes for a ping to travel from the chip to multiple trusted “landmark” servers around the world and back. [Kyle Miller](https://cset.georgetown.edu/staff/kyle-miller/), a senior research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report, says that for new AI chips, manufacturers could integrate PLV functionality into the hardware itself, while a firmware update could be applied to chips already in circulation.

Not all AI chips should be tracked, the researchers note. “The priority should be for the highest-end data-center chips—the cream of the crop in high-end data-center GPUs,” says [Jacob Feldgoise](https://cset.georgetown.edu/staff/jacob-feldgoise/), a senior data-research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report.

A similar initiative involves transmitting encrypted “[sovereignty certificates](https://github.com/Lucid-Computing/sovereignty-certificate-specification).” These certificates act as “cryptographic credentials that provide verifiable, unforgeable proof of the physical location of a computing device, such as a CPU or GPU, at a specific point in time,” per the [draft specification](https://github.com/Lucid-Computing/sovereignty-certificate-specification/blob/main/spec/sovereignty-certificates.md) published by secure computing firm [Lucid Computing](https://lucidcomputing.ai/).

“If you can use a private key that exists on a particular chip, and you can sign a message with that cryptographic key, and then that message is received by a so-called landmark server, then you can send a couple of those messages and time those messages. A lot of modern chips come with [trusted execution environments](https://spectrum.ieee.org/data-privacy) that support a hardware root of trust where you can sign these messages,” says [Kristian Rönn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kristianronn), CEO and cofounder of Lucid Computing. “You get a radius of where the chip has to be.”

PLV could have some effect on chip smugglers, Miller says. “They know if they turn this chip on, it’s going to start pinging these landmark servers. That could deter some smuggling.” And when the system flags a chip as residing in a unintended location, “the PLV data gives you a better sense of when and where it was moved,” he adds.

However, ping-based location verification can only uncover diversion after it has happened. It can’t track offline chips that are in storage, in transit, or have yet to be activated. And when a chip fails to respond to a ping request, the system won’t know whether it’s due to a valid reason or nefarious causes.

This is where physical inspections come in. “You need to do that follow-on investigative work. You need to physically go to these data centers and do those physical audits as well. Essentially, [PLV] generates leads, and you track down those leads,” says Miller.

A PLV system involves sending signals from a chip to and from trusted servers and measuring the travel time.Source image: CSET

## A “lie detector” for data centers

Despite the safeguards around ping-based location verification, the methodology remains vulnerable to particular attacks. If adversaries gain physical access to a chip, for example, they could prevent it from sending signals, or they could extract cryptographic keys and spoof a signal from the intended location.

To fight that, some security researchers are exploring hardware fingerprints instead of cryptographic keys. One study demonstrated a proof-of-concept [GPU fingerprinting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01930) function that produced unique fingerprints for Nvidia H200 GPUs based on their manufacturing variations and random numbers as seeds.

“You want to support other types of fingerprinting because not all chips have a hardware root of trust. You might want to use some statistical fingerprinting to know that the chip is what it’s supposed to be,” Rönn says. “It also requires good physical security around the chips, such as tamper-proofing. Over time, you ideally want to have more defense in depth.”

Additionally, the CSET report warns that PLV is costly. And if China achieves the ability to craft its own advanced AI chips, “then tracking the export of U.S. chips is less of a strategic priority,” says Miller.

[Hanna Dohmen](https://cset.georgetown.edu/staff/hanna-dohmen/), a senior research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report, points to other gaps in the U.S. export-control regime. “Currently, Chinese companies are legally able to [remotely access AI chips](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/) abroad through cloud-service providers,” she says. These advanced AI chips might be installed in data centers across Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia, which are [increasingly serving Chinese firms](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/business/malaysia-data-center-china.html).

Whether or not a “Find My” for AI chips becomes a regulatory requirement, Feldgoise envisions tighter conditions for the export of advanced AI chips. “This is based on the increasing importance of compute to national and economic security,” he says. “The chips that generate compute are being seen as a strategic resource, so I would be unsurprised if the due diligence requirements on these devices increase as time passes.”

Rönn views sovereignty certificates as essential tools in the future, likening it to a “lie detector” for data centers that answers the “where, how, what, and who questions for us to know that they comply with a basic standard of security when it comes to AI systems.”

items.title: A single AI model simulates the behavior of many substances, from sliding sand to folding proteins
items.content:
Today, a scientist who wants to simulate a physical process must pick the right tool for that one job, such as a solver built for flowing water or another designed to model the way a protein folds. Each one is hand-coded around the specific equations that dictate how that process behaves.

Researchers at MIT, the University of British Columbia (UBC), and elsewhere have now replaced that patchwork with a single deep-learning system, called [WorldParticle](https://worldparticle.github.io/WorldParticle_Web/#top), that could help engineers model different physical phenomena, from sliding sand to folding proteins, with one unified artificial intelligence architecture.

Scientists and engineers could use this system to model processes that typically require separate simulators, such as a fluid sloshing against a deformable solid. This could offer a faster, more accurate way to simulate how sloshing oil might impact an elastic valve in a storage tank, for instance. It could also help engineers study where and how granular materials, like sand or soil, could move when a soft robot touches them.

The system represents every material it simulates, from a dune of sand to a protein molecule, as tiny particles and predicts where those particles will move one step at a time. Because it learns the underlying dynamics rather than being programmed with an equation, the model can adapt to materials, forces, and environments it never encountered during training.

In the long term, the researchers hope this work helps scientists discover new materials and explore physical processes they would be unable to effectively study with existing simulation methods.

“We want to have a GPT moment for simulation,” says Peter Yichen Chen, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at UBC, and is a co-corresponding author of an open-access [paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.15305) on this technique. “Every time people want to build a simulator for a particular physical phenomenon, they need to code it up from scratch. Our vision is to have a foundation model that works out of the box for any scenario you want to simulate. This is a first step in that direction.”

Chen is joined by co-corresponding and co-lead author Minghao Guo, an MIT postdoc; co-lead authors Caoliwen Wang and Siyuan Chen, UBC graduate students; Wojciech Matusik, an MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science who leads the Computational Design and Fabrication Group within the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL); and others at UBC, Georgia Tech, Inria, Meta, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Utah, the University of California at Los Angeles, and the University of Hong Kong. The research will be presented at the ACM SIGGRAPH Conference and Exhibition on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques in Asia.

**Unified simulation**

For this work, the researchers drew inspiration from world models. These powerful AI systems learn the rules that govern the physical world so they can predict how objects or environments will change over time in response to certain actions or conditions.

The researchers applied these concepts to develop a unified AI architecture that can simulate multiple types of physical phenomena.

“If you study deformable objects and fluids, you would need two simulators — one for each physical regime. But if you unify them into one model, maybe you could couple the physics of these two processes and gain insights into new problems?” Guo says.

WorldParticle breaks an object into thousands or millions of tiny, three-dimensional dots, or particles, using what is known as a Lagrangian representation. It tracks the movement and velocity of the particles over space and time to simulate the material’s dynamics.

Typically, when scientists model materials and physical processes using Lagrangian particles, they use a governing equation that defines the fundamental laws which control how that material behaves over time and space. They must convert that complex equation into a formula a numerical solver can handle, repeating these steps for each material and process they want to model.

Instead, the researchers designed a neural network that learns to solve governing equations in general, eliminating the need to design a new model and solver to handle each one.

Once WorldParticle converts an object into particles, a neural network takes the 3D positions and physical properties of the particles as inputs. It outputs their positions and properties for the next frame of the simulation, predicting the material’s motion over time and space in one-second increments.

“It is a similar architecture to ChatGPT. But instead of predicting one word at a time to write a piece of text, we are predicting how these particles will move, one step at a time,” Chen says.

Before each simulation step, WorldParticle separates the external forces that affect the physical system, like impulse forces that affect an ocean wave when it slams into a seawall.

After predicting the initial states of the particles, WorldParticle integrates the external forces back into the simulation, correcting its particle predictions based on how those forces affect the object’s behavior. In this way, the system can generalize to unseen materials, changing environmental conditions, and varied forces.

**A general, scalable framework**

But because a complex object could be broken into millions of particles, the problem quickly becomes too computationally intensive for the model to handle.

To streamline processing, the researchers employed a merging technique to combine and compress particles while still allowing WorldParticle to capture fine-grained details of their behavior.

“We needed to do a lot of detailed engineering and employ many tweaks to the architecture for it to be truly generalizable and scalable,” Guo says.

They demonstrated WorldParticle by modeling six different physical phenomena, including deformable objects, granular materials, and proteins, with higher accuracy than numerical simulation methods.

For instance, WorldParticle effectively captured how a granular object would collapse into a pile while some baseline methods left sand particles floating in the air. Their method also modeled how protein structures change over time about 100 times faster than numerical simulators, Guo adds.

The general-purpose framework could be applied to many materials and processes, including soft robot manipulation tasks, RNA evolution, and astrophysical phenomena like the merging of galaxies, the researchers say.

Moving forward, they want to adapt WorldParticle to simulate these and other physical systems. They also want to build on this work toward the development of a full, general-purpose simulation pipeline for scientific discovery.

“We see the unification of computation and science giving us new insights and tools to discover physical phenomena or explain some unexplainable physical phenomena,” Guo says. “With a unified model, we could unlock many discoveries that we can’t even imagine.”

items.title: AI-assisted learning platform helps robots reason beyond literal commands
items.content:
Humans are intuitive by nature. We can sense meaning beyond the literal words that we encounter. Now, a new artificial intelligence-assisted learning platform developed by MIT engineers is enabling robots to read larger meaning into a human’s natural language commands.

In a study to be presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning this month, researchers from MIT and New York University introduce [FLEX](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.28893), a flexible feature-editing pipeline for robot motion-planning.

With FLEX, humans can interact with a robot by giving it instructions in natural, conversational language. The robot can not only follow the instructions literally but also read into the words to draw larger generalizations that help to improve its motion-planning task.

The team demonstrated FLEX in several simulated scenarios, including one in which a robot serves a cup of coffee. In these virtual scenarios, a person interacts with a robotic arm by typing commands in natural language. As the robot moves the coffee cup over a cluttered table, the person might type “Don’t spill on the laptop!” In response, the robot will reason about why it should avoid the laptop. For this, FLEX incorporates a large language model (LLM) — a type of AI system that is trained on enormous libraries of text, including social media posts, video transcriptions, and web content, which the LLM uses to identify larger trends, patterns, and generalizations.

“LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet,” says study author Nathan Dennler, a postdoc in MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). “People might have written about, ‘Oh, my phone dropped in the water and now it doesn’t work,’ or ‘I spilled coffee on my computer and now it doesn’t work.’ So LLMs pick up on the idea that liquids plus devices leads to things not working.”

Through the LLM, the robot reasons that it should also avoid bumping into all electronics. In its updated path, the robot adjusts to avoid both the laptop and a nearby phone, without the person having to explicitly spell this out.

“The idea is that there is some higher-level intention behind the words that you say,” Dennler says. “People naturally get this. But you have to carefully explain that to a robot, which takes time and effort. FLEX gives you an interface of communication with a robot to say, ‘When people say this, they mean that.’”

The study was led by Andreea Bobu, assistant professor of aeronautics and astronautics at MIT. Co-authors are Audrey Lee SM ’26 and Ilia Sucholutsky of New York University.

**Beyond what we say**

At MIT, Bobu heads up the Collaborative Learning and Autonomy Research (CLEAR) Lab, where her group develops autonomous agents that learn to work for, with, and around people. She is focused on developing assistive and household robots that can carry out physical tasks, and reason and adapt in real-time, in response to a person’s natural, conversational commands.

“Robots use math to do their trajectory planning. But we can’t expect a consumer to learn to do this math in order to tell a robot what to do,” says Dennler, who is a member of the CLEAR Lab. “Instead of having to get people to learn how to use a robot in a specific way, the goal is to interact with the robot through natural language.”

There is a large effort in the robotics community to incorporate natural language into robotic learning pipelines. Various strategies include using language to clarify a task’s goal, redirect a robot’s trajectory, and update its understanding of what is a safe path to take. These existing methods use natural language to tell the robot how to physically perform a task. But a robot could potentially learn much more from what we tell it.

Bobu and her colleagues are expanding what robots can learn from natural language commands. In their new study, they focused on enabling a robot to interpret a person’s underlying, unspecified preference from limited natural language commands.

**Absorbing common sense**

The team’s new robot learning platform, FLEX, is a three-step process that helps a robot read more into a natural language command, beyond what it is explicitly told to do.

The first step, “Add,” instructs a robot to add a feature to its list of things in its environment that matter for the task at hand, based on a user’s natural language command. For instance, as a robot is moving a bowling ball from one location to another, a person might interject with “Don’t drop it on my mug!” The robot would then add the mug to a list of things to avoid in its path. This first step is how previous methods have worked. Every time a person makes a correction, the robot adds to its features list, and updates its trajectory to avoid those features.

“The problem happens when your feature list becomes super long, and some features are no longer relevant because your environment may have changed,” says Dennler, who notes that this approach can grow tiresome if a person has to specify every specific feature to avoid.

The second step, “Generalize,” is the new solution that FLEX provides. This step incorporates an LLM — in this case, GPT-4o — that considers the mug, along with any other features that the person has so far specified to avoid. The LLM automatically searches through its vast cache of data for patterns and connections among these features, to ultimately make a generalization that it should avoid objects that are fragile, even when the person has not explicitly said so.

“LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet, from all sorts of people and places,” Dennler says. “Because they’ve trained so much on those things, some of that common sense gets absorbed into the LLM.”

In the third step, “Mask,” the robot’s standard computer vision system assesses its environment to determine what objects are no longer present, and then deletes those objects from its features list. This entire three-step process takes about five seconds.

The team tested FLEX in simulations of a robot arm carrying out three different tasks: serving a cup of coffee, moving a candle, and carrying a bowling ball. In all three scenarios, volunteers interacted with the virtual robot by typing natural language commands, such as “Don’t spill on my laptop,” “Stay away from the stack of paper,” and “Don’t drop on the mug.” With FLEX, the robot followed all three commands literally and also reasoned at a higher level to not spill on electronics, stay away from flammable objects, and not drop its cargo on fragile things.

“Everyone’s homes are different, and everyone cares about different things, so no robot comes out of the box knowing what matters to you,” Bobu says. “What excites me about FLEX is that it can pick that up from a sentence or two instead of asking you to spell out every rule — and that’s the difference between a robot people put up with and one they actually want in their home.”****

This work was partly supported by the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium and the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing’s Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing program.

items.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
items.content:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo

Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

items.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
items.content:
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

[See My World](https://www.eventbrite.co.uk/e/see-my-world-film-festival-tickets-2000609164867), a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

items.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
items.content:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security.

The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both [Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/us-public-sector-customer-awards-announcement-2024/) and [public](https://www.highergov.com/contract-opportunity/chainalysis-enterprise-subscription-support-5000217691-u-48ee6/) [sources](https://www.getwab.com/index.php/library/vendors/chainalysis-inc-cage-7dje5) have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.

## We regret to inform you...

Last Friday, Chainalysis [said](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/security-incident-october-30/) it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It's not clear why the company considered such information "non-sensitive."

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/chainalysis-says-hackers-stole-credentials-and-tokens-for-all-of-its-customers/)
