They need the monazite. And if we can supply the monazite, that’s sort of a natural, right?”

It probably won’t happen, though. The logic of rare-earth mining is utterly different from the logic of mining a commodity like, say, copper. Multiple experts contacted by **Spectrum** suggested that the cost of developing a monazite mine at Alces Lake, including such necessary infrastructure as roadways, electricity, and water, would be in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Such costs, and the mercurial exigencies of the rare-earths market, make it unlikely that the government of Saskatchewan would commit that kind of money, even with help from the Canadian federal government. These factors help explain why Canada, which has some of the most attractive deposits of rare-earth ores on the planet, along with impressive mining companies and resources, has no operating mines for rare earths.

Meanwhile, SRC is pursuing other options. Under a deal announced in May with [REalloys](https://realloys.com/), in Euclid, Ohio, REalloys will spend $20.6 million for upgrades to SRC’s Saskatoon facility, while SRC develops technology to produce rare-earth metals from rare-earth oxides. The deal also gives REalloys the right to purchase up to 80 percent of the SRC plant’s output. Where will the feedstock come from? Hard to say, but REalloys also struck a deal with [U.S. Critical Materials Corp.](https://uscriticalmaterials.com/) for 10 percent of the hypothetical output of a proposed mine at Sheep Creek, in Montana. Sheep Creek reportedly has substantial amounts of hard-rock monazite that’s unusually low in thorium. But it’s far from certain that those deposits will ever be mined. The proposal for developing a mine there, in a [breathtakingly scenic](https://flyfishingjourneys.com/the-breathtaking-beauty-of-the-bitterroot-river-montana/) area near the headwaters of the Bitterroot River, has attracted [fierce opposition](https://dailymontanan.com/2025/12/02/sheep-creek-mine-exploration-in-bitterroot-draws-opposition/) from [environmental groups](https://www.montanarightnow.com/montana/debate-grows-over-sheep-creek-rare-earth-project-in-the-bitterroot/article_e984d74b-d611-498f-95d9-ff4e8592a72d.html), [outdoor enthusiasts](https://fieldandstream.com/stories/conservation/public-lands-and-waters/montanans-oppose-controversial-mine-above-bitterroot-headwaters), and [local officials](https://zinke.house.gov/media/press-releases/zinke-sheehy-statements-proposed-sheep-creek-mine).

Taken together, SRC’s recent moves have left industry veterans nonplussed. “I’m not sure what their business model is,” said one. “They say, ‘we’re a research institute. Our mandate is to help industry.’ The reality is, they’re competing with industry.”

SRC has also drawn scrutiny for some questionable business practices. In 2022, SRC board member Dennis Fitzpatrick [was fired after raising concerns](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RBMDoswuGK8) about the qualifications of an engineer hired to manage and direct operations at SRC’s Saskatoon plant. The president and CEO of SRC at the time, Mike Crabtree, was responsible for the hire. [A subsequent investigation](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatchewan/minister-jeremy-harrison-fired-crown-corp-board-chair-who-blew-the-whistle-on-apparent-conflicts-of-interest-1.7352049) of Fitzpatrick’s claims by the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. detailed a troubling web of relationships and practices surrounding the SRC’s rare-earths initiative. (Fitzpatrick did not respond to multiple emails.) For example, past business associates of Crabtree’s were reportedly appointed to positions of authority without any other candidates being considered and without their connections to Crabtree being made public.

In one case, in 2021, Crabtree disclosed that he was offering a venture capital firm, Westbridge Capital, an opportunity to invest in the rare-earths plant. But according to Fitzpatrick, Crabtree never mentioned that the VC firm was run by an SRC board member who also happened to be one of Crabtree’s business associates—or that Crabtree himself was a trustee of Westbridge and an investor in the company, as well as a paid advisor.

Crabtree remains as SRC’s CEO.

## Managing Toxic By-products From Rare Earths

Putting aside SRC’s missteps, the organization does have one advantage: It holds multiple licenses from the [Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission](https://www.cnsc-ccsn.gc.ca/eng/) to handle, process, and manage radioactive materials. And that’s huge.

Most of the radioactive burden associated with processing monazite ore comes from substances produced during processing. In one of the early steps, pulverized, powdery ore is dried and then leached in strong acids—a process called cracking—to produce a rare-earth concentrate. Waste products of this step include a slurry containing thorium hydroxide and much smaller amounts of uranium hydroxide. The rare-earth concentrate then undergoes an extraction process to isolate specific rare earths, such as neodymium or dysprosium. More [thorium](https://www.smenet.org/What-We-Do/Technical-Briefings/Thorium-as-a-Byproduct-of-Rare-Earth-Element-Produ) and also radium are produced during these steps.

Waste barrels were photographed in 2024 at Energy Fuels’ White Mesa Mill, where ores containing uranium and rare-earths are processed and refined.Jesse Rieser/The New York Times/Redux

The thorium hydroxide slurry, meanwhile, is typically deposited in heavily regulated waste cells, called tailings impoundments or tailings ponds. The thorium hydroxide, either in the form of a slurry or a powder, must be stored in isolation from the environment indefinitely. Energy Fuels stores waste from its longstanding uranium production operations, as well as its new rare-earth operations, in tailings impoundments at its White Mesa Mill facility. The impoundments are just 10 kilometers from the community center of the [Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, a group of Indigenous people](https://www.utemountainutetribe.com/), which has [vigorously opposed](https://insideclimatenews.org/news/10072026/arizona-raises-uranium-mine-contaminant-limits/) operations at White Mesa Mill for [more than 20 years](https://icmagazine.org/the-ute-mountain-ute-tribe-is-paying-the-price-of-nuclear-colonialism/).

Virtually all of the thorium is the isotope thorium-232, which is only weakly radioactive. Its radiation is alpha particles, which cannot penetrate human skin. Nevertheless, improper storage can have serious consequences, particularly if the thorium is inhaled or ingested.

“Have a look at the gravitational separation of HMS [heavy mineral sands] in Nigeria,” [Thomas Kruemmer](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tkruemmer/), a rare-earth consultant and analyst, wrote in an email. “There is lots of dust in the Nigerian processing sites, which the workers inevitably breathe in. And inside your respiratory system there **isn’t** any protective skin, so alpha radiation develops its full potential. This is something many people do not consider.”

In 2012, protestors in Malaysia [top] rallied against the Lynas rare earths processing facility [above], then under construction near Kuantan. Left: AFP/Getty Images; Right: Goh Seng Chong/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Moreover, adds Kruemmer, “it is not thorium itself. It is the decay isotopes of thorium that are highly radioactive.” One decay product of thorium is polonium, he points out, “the preferred poison for [killing] [Russian dissidents](https://www.npr.org/2021/09/21/1039224996/russia-alexander-litvinenko-european-court-human-rights-putin).”

In 1982, a company called Asia Rare Earth, a subsidiary of [Mitsubishi Chemical](https://www.mcgc.com/english/), began extracting yttrium from monazite ore in Perak, Malaysia. Local residents soon began complaining of various illnesses. With the consent of the Malaysian government, the company had built a waste channel to a nearby disposal site, where the waste was stored in open steel barrels and in an unlined waste pond. The waste overflowed from the pond whenever it rained heavily. In 1984, a Japanese professor measured radiation levels at and near the pond and found them to be, in the most extreme cases, [hundreds of times higher](https://consumer.org.my/chronology-of-events-in-the-bukit-merah-asian-rare-earth-development/) than internationally accepted maximums. A subsequent investigation found extremely [high levels of birth defects](https://www.nytimes.com/2011/03/09/business/energy-environment/09rareside.html) and eight cases of leukemia in the [small community near the waste dump](https://youtu.be/BKJnbvtjjfQ?si=Eq8xd-THyibspx0i).

In 2011, at age 69, Lai Kwan prepared to bathe her 29-year-old son, Cheah Kok Leong [top]. Cheah Kok was born with severe mental disabilities that Lai Kwan believed were caused by exposure to radiation that she received while working at a rare earths processing plant in Bukit Merah, Malaysia [bottom, photographed during its disassembly].Rahman Roslan/The New York Times/Redux

A protracted legal fight among local residents and Asia Rare Earth and the Malaysian government culminated in the closure of the plant in 1992. By that time, so much radioactive material had been carelessly dumped that cleanup took more than two decades and cost Mitsubishi an estimated $100 million. The episode still haunts the rare-earths industry in Malaysia, where Lynas now processes monazite concentrate at the [largest rare earths processing facility](https://www.straitstimes.com/asia/se-asia/delicate-extraction-malaysia-offers-rare-earths-alternative-to-china) in the world. That plant, in Kuantan in the state of Pahang, has been the subject of organized and active local opposition that began even before its commissioning in 2012. The Malaysian government has sporadically [tightened its regulations on the plant](https://www.asiapacific.ca/publication/what-canada-can-learn-about-critical-minerals-from-australian-firm), stipulating that, for example, radioactive wastes be shipped out of Malaysia or that the processing stages that create radioactive residues be accomplished outside of Malaysia.

Kennedy notes that if monazite ore is to become a major source of rare earths, much larger quantities of thorium will need to be disposed, probably more than could be economically accommodated in lined and isolated tailings ponds.

One of the very few options for using such large amounts of thorium involves nuclear power. Years ago, countries including the U.S., Canada, Norway, and Germany had thorium-reactor research programs, and India has had a slow-moving program for decades. But today, the only operating thorium power reactor is in China. The Shanghai Institute of Applied Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has been operating, since 2023, a [2-megawatt molten-salt-cooled reactor](https://spectrum.ieee.org/chinas-thorium-molten-salt-reactor) that is thorium-fueled.

The world’s only operating thorium reactor is a 2-megawatt unit at the Shanghai Institute of Applied Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. In October 2025, technicians used mechanical arms to analyze samples of the reactor’s molten-salt fuel.Jin Liwang/Xinhua/Getty Images

A couple of Western startups are keeping the thorium reactor dream alive. A Franco-Dutch company called [Thorizon](https://www.thorizon.com/about-us) says it has designed a reactor that would be fueled by a mixture of thorium and spent nuclear fuel. Startup [Copenhagen Atomics](https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/articles/copenhagen-atomics-secures-thorium-supply-from-norway) is working on a 1-MW reactor that’s a prototype for a 100-MW, mass-manufacturable, molten-salt reactor.

Processing of monazite ore could provide fuel for an enormous number of thorium reactors far into the future. Consider a single large facility producing 5,000 tonnes of rare-earth oxide a year. If the monazite contains 7 percent thorium, the plant would also be producing roughly 700 tonnes of thorium a year. According to [Rusty Towell](https://acu.edu/faculty/rusty-towell/), a professor at [Abilene Christian University](https://acu.edu/) in Texas who directs an advanced-reactor project there, a tonne of thorium would be sufficient to generate about 350 MW (electric) for a year. So the large processing facility alone would be throwing off enough thorium annually to keep 2,450 100-MW reactors operating for a year.

That amount of power—245 gigawatts—is [about half](https://www.statista.com/statistics/504369/electric-power-sector-capacity-in-the-us-forecast/) of **all** the generating capacity growth forecast for the United States over the next decade, a period during which analysts expect accelerating electricity growth due to increasing numbers of data centers and electric vehicles.

## What Could Strangle Rare-Earth Supply Chains?

Virtually all rare-earths experts foresee a growing role for monazite. But given the problems with thorium, local opposition to some projects, and political instabilities connected to others, some have muted expectations. “The sole and single monazite hope rests with Iluka’s expensive project in Australia, IMHO,” writes Kruemmer. [Iluka Resources](https://www.iluka.com/), based in Perth, is now building a [massive rare-earths refining facility](https://www.iluka.com/operations-resource-development/resource-development/eneabba/) at Eneabba, 275 km north of Perth. [It will process](https://rare-earth-mining.com/iluka-resources/) a million-tonne monazite stockpile that accumulated over decades from the company’s other mining operations. The cost of the project is estimated at AU $1.8 billion (about US $1.3 billion).

In a US $1.3 billion project, Iluka Resources is building a massive facility in Eneabba, Australia, to extract and separate rare earths from a million-tonne stockpile of monazite, visible in the background of this photo.Iluka Resources

For other experts, though, the biggest challenges facing monazite projects isn’t thorium, or radiation, or regulations. It’s the blend of quirks, misconceptions, and self-dealing that dog the entire rare-earths industry.

“The rare-earth mining business is the Afghanistan of mining,” quips Kennedy. It’s a place where people and companies go with grand ideas, only to become ensnared in quagmires.

One fundamental problem is the highly speculative nature of almost every aspect of the rare-earths business, which lends itself to backroom deals. In particular, the industry is plagued by speculators who buy stakes in a project with no intention of staying with the project through completion; they cash out as soon as they can profit from any future favorable news—a technique known as “pump and dump.”

Consider the Trump administration’s[](https://www.ft.com/content/0a337dc3-5a12-4c82-87b5-f2340378006c?syn-25a6b1a6=1)decision to take a 10 percent stake in USA Rare Earth [in exchange for $277 million](https://www.ft.com/content/0a337dc3-5a12-4c82-87b5-f2340378006c?syn-25a6b1a6=1) and to provide a $1.3 billion secured loan to the company. USA Rare Earth has the rights to a deposit called Round Top near Sierra Blanca, Texas. The company [hired the Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald](https://www.ft.com/content/4ba88e38-fdfd-447c-9250-163cd85293c4?syn-25a6b1a6=1) to raise $1 billion in equity financing for the deal. Cantor Fitzgerald, as it happens, is run by the sons of Howard Lutnick, Donald Trump’s Commerce Secretary.

Meanwhile, there is no rare-earths mine at Round Top, and it’s a distinct possibility that [there never will be](https://nightmarketresearch.com/usar/).

“The current administration consistently fails to seek expert advice and is recklessly pouring billions of taxpayer dollars into speculative [rare-earth element] processes and projects, like Round Top, that have little chance of commercial success,” says [Terry McNulty](https://www.cim.org/past-award-winners/terence-p-mcnulty/), a mining consultant based in Tucson.

[Geoff Atkins](https://investornews.com/critical-minerals-rare-earths/world-renowned-rare-earths-expert-geoff-atkins-to-join-the-critical-minerals-institute-board/), vice president of business development of the Canadian rare-earths firm [Ucore Rare Metals](https://ucore.com/), [had advice for his colleagues](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TwTv8JwU2yE) at a convention of the Critical Minerals Institute in 2022. “Instead of focusing on your speculative value,” he said, “instead of being able to say we’ve got the biggest project in the world, instead of, ‘we’ve got a [net present value] of $3 billion or $4 billion,’ how about you say, ‘we’ve got a project which is going to get into operation, and this operation is going to provide the greatest value to our shareholders in the long term, not just in the short term when we can pump this up and, you know, the [early] investors can sell out.

“Because unless there is that shift,” he warned, “we’re not going to have any hope of getting the volumes we need to give the certainty to the downstream supply chain.”

In short, the rare-earths industry outside of China needs to grow up. And sooner rather than later.

*This article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Can a Radioactive Ore Break China’s Grip on Rare Earths?”*

items.title: U.S. Chip Firms Bet Big on R&D
items.content:
On 12 October, [Applied Materials](https://www.appliedmaterials.com) unveiled a multibillion-dollar research facility in Sunnyvale, Calif., in the heart of [Silicon Valley](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/silicon-valley). The company [first announced in 2023](https://www.appliedmaterials.com/us/en/epic.html) plans to invest US $4 billion in its Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization (EPIC) Center, but now [says](https://ir.appliedmaterials.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-materials-and-kioxia-partner-epic-center-advance-next) it will invest even more: about $5 billion. The boost is part of a wider growth in private investment that is both enlarging the U.S. semiconductor R&D sector and making it more complex.

The EPIC announcement follows others, in August, by two semiconductor firms. Memory chipmaker Micron disclosed that it [would invest $10 billion](https://investors.micron.com/news/press-release/2026/Micron-Unveils-Micron-Research-Labs-a-U-S--Based-Long-Horizon-Innovation-Hub-to-Shape-the-Future-of-Memory-and-AI/default.aspx) over 10 years at its Boise, Idaho, memory research lab, and SK Hynix said it will spend [$4 billion on an advanced packaging facility](https://news.skhynix.com/en/groundbreaking-ceremony-in-indiana/) in West Lafayette, Ind. (Neither of those companies responded to *IEEE Spectrum*’s questions about how much of those funds would be for R&D.)

The U.S. federal government has [encouraged investment](https://consumerelectronicsdaily.com/chip-supply/chips-act-semiconductor-investment/) in U.S. semiconductor research by chip giants based in friendly nations, such as TSMC and Samsung. It has also enacted tariffs on foreign components and put some of its own money into faltering domestic chip companies including [Intel](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/newsroom/news/corporate/intel-and-trump-administration-reach-historic-agreement.html). But the real motive behind today’s wave of private investment, according to some analysts and executives, is that companies anticipate enormous profits from feeding the current AI frenzy. “The best explanation is probably not about policy or politics and probably more about a big jump in revenue growth driven by AI demand,” says [Chris Miller](https://fletcher.tufts.edu/academics/faculty/christopher-miller) of Tufts University, and author of the book [**Chip War**](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Chip-War/Chris-Miller/9781982172015).

## AI Money, Tools Accelerate Chipmaking

Applied Materials’ chief strategy officer [Tristan Holtam](https://www.appliedmaterials.com/us/en/about/leadership/executive-team/tristan-holtam.html) agrees: “It’s really all about AI.” The firm estimates that the top 10 semiconductor companies’ revenue has grown about 150 percent since 2021 thanks to AI demand, and they have in turn raised their investment in R&D by 67 percent, he says. Those top semiconductor companies are collectively investing $67 billion this year in R&D, Holtam adds, dwarfing federal funding. Most of that federal money comes from the [2022 CHIPS and Science Act](https://spectrum.ieee.org/chips-act-of-2022), which [allocated $11 billion for R&D](https://spectrum.ieee.org/chips-act-impact-semiconductor-manufacturing) over several years.

While demand for AI-ready chips provides funding and motivation for more chip R&D, AI in the form of research tools is helping the people actually doing the R&D. [Entegris](https://www.entegris.com/en/home/about-us/corporate-overview.html), a semiconductor materials science company headquartered in Billerica, Mass., is applying AI in its early-stage research and design, says [Olivier Blachier](https://www.entegris.com/en/home/about-us/corporate-overview/olivier-blachier.html), the company’s chief innovation officer. At his company, workers are defining performance goals for next-generation products and asking AI tools to suggest promising new materials to match. “If you’re an AI engineer, a chemist, a materials scientist, you can combine scientific understanding with AI-driven modeling and simulation to work backward from a target performance requirement,” he says. The company is also piloting AI for preliminary screening of potential new materials, similar to what the [pharmaceutical industry](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12298131/) does with new molecules before trying to synthesize and evaluate materials in the lab.

At Applied Materials, Holtam reports that the company is making use of AI-enabled acceleration in new material discovery, generative design of equipment, and algorithm and software development. “The timing is perfect for EPIC,” Applied Materials’ new lab devoted to equipment and processes, he declares.

An artist’s rendering depicts Applied Materials’ new $5 billion EPIC research center, which was opened on 12 October 2026.Applied Materials

## Reshaping Chip R&D, Not Just Resizing It

Physical proximity is emerging as a key advantage for chipmakers, and that is reshaping the industry’s geographic and facilities investments. The Japanese semiconductor packaging company Resonac [opened its first R&D facility in the U.S.](https://www.resonac.com/news/2026/04/20/3803.html) in April, for example. “These companies have a very strong reason to want to be close to their customers and close to their customers’ customers so they can make the right investments for the next five to 10 years,” according to Miller.

The knowledge of how prototype chipmaking equipment works does not move up and down the supply chain as easily as software. “The traditional way of working to get brand new technology into the hands of our customers, the chipmakers, was to ship a prototype piece of equipment from our lab into their pilot line. That’s a kind of heart-in-your-mouth type of situation,” Holtam says.

“That was always a huge point of contention,” he adds. “At what level of maturity we’re willing to allow a prototype outside of our building when the chip company is pulling on that as hard as possible.” Applied Materials analyzed 15 years of its own internal R&D to look for the places likely to benefit from fewer such heart-stopping shipments and from more shoulder-to-shoulder lab work. Then it conducted pilot programs of its customer-in-the-lab approach and got what Holtam deemed “very, very encouraging results.”

That helped prompt Applied Materials to invite top customers to set up shop inside the new EPIC lab. So far, [TSMC](https://ir.appliedmaterials.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-materials-and-tsmc-partner-epic-center-accelerate-ai), [Samsung](https://www.appliedmaterials.com/us/en/epic.html), [Micron](https://ir.appliedmaterials.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-materials-and-micron-partner-advance-us-innovation-next), [Broadcom](https://futurumgroup.com/insights/applied-materials-epic-advanced-packaging-ecosystem-adds-broadcom-to-tsmc/), and others have said yes. Even competing customers will get their own facilities under EPIC’s roof, with digital firewalls, physical barriers, and other security features. “We’re eliminating handoffs,” Holtam says, and making it easier for their own research staff to give customers a preview of what’s coming.

Applied Materials’ [stated goal](https://ir.appliedmaterials.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-materials-launches-multibillion-dollar-rd-platform) is for its EPIC center to reduce, by several years, the time it takes to go from early-stage discoveries to chip commercialization. That’s typically a 10- to 15-year process.

The U.S. Department of Commerce announced similar goals for [big-tent semiconductor R&D facilities](https://spectrum.ieee.org/nstc) under the CHIPS Act, but those are now [behind schedule](https://spectrum.ieee.org/chips-act-impact-semiconductor-manufacturing) or indefinitely paused. They might have helped startups [get a leg up](https://spectrum.ieee.org/power-electronics) on the chip giants in a notoriously concentrated industry. Indeed, EPIC’s partnership announcements so far have been with other industry leaders, so startups may be at the back of the queue. Right now, generally, Blachier says, “small and medium companies have to cooperate with bigger companies to feed into the giants.”

Another way the industry is seeking acceleration is by [closer ties with universities](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-chip-design-fab-ucla). Universities also serve as a bridge to the U.S. national semiconductor research strategy since universities have long-running research funding partnerships with the federal government.

“There is a benefit in having longer-term horizons and supported investments,” Blachier says, referring to EU and some Asian countries’ national chip strategies, which have created successful precompetitive research facilities such as [Imec](https://www.imec-int.com/en). More facilities like that in the U.S., he says, would be “definitely useful, and tend to benefit the ecosystem.”

items.title: The U.S. Just Bet $1 Billion on Quantum Chip Manufacturing
items.content:
The U.S. Department of Commerce has finalized a [CHIPS and Science Act](https://spectrum.ieee.org/chips-act-of-2022) R&D award of up to $1 billion for Anderon, a quantum foundry IBM established earlier this year. The 16 September [announcement](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/09/department-commerce-announces-finalization-chips-rd-award-anderon) backs a manufacturing service for IBM and other quantum-hardware developers.

[IBM is matching the award](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-09-16-anderon,-an-ibm-company,-finalizes-agreement-with-the-u-s-department-of-commerce-for-a-1-billion-chips-award-to-accelerate-r-d-for-u-s-based-pure-play-quantum-foundry) with US $1 billion in cash and contributing intellectual property, assets, and skilled workers. Headquartered in Albany, N.Y., Anderon builds on an existing operation at Albany NanoTech, where IBM has made quantum wafers for more than five years, says [CEO Mukesh Khare](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mvkhare/). That existing infrastructure has helped Anderon get started: Its first wafers are already moving through a production-scale, 300-millimeter line.

Quantum computing “is moving from science to real commercial impact now,” Khare says. “That means the industry also needs a more stable manufacturing source for building quantum chips.”

If Anderon is successful, it could do for quantum hardware what Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) did for conventional chips: Let companies focus on designing chips without each one having to build a multibillion-dollar factory for the underlying hardware.

## What an Automated Quantum Fab Can Offer

IBM says shifting much of its quantum wafer R&D from the 200-millimeter fabrication lab at the IBM Research headquarters in Yorktown Heights, N.Y., to the Albany 300-millimeter line, beginning in 2021, doubled chip-development speed and increased its chips’ physical complexity tenfold. Round-the-clock processing shortened fabrication cycles, and advanced manufacturing techniques enabled more elaborate wiring and qubit connections. Anderon draws on Albany NanoTech’s manufacturing capability and IBM’s experience deploying more than 90 quantum systems since 2016. The challenge now is extending those capabilities to outside designers. Anderon’s potential customers include processor developers without fabs, system builders, and national laboratories. Even companies with their own manual chipmaking facilities may be interested in outsourcing fabrication to an automated foundry. Rigetti Computing, for example, another [CHIPS Act R&D award winner](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/09/department-commerce-announces-finalization-chips-rd-award-rigetti), is in talks with Anderon, according to [CEO Subodh Kulkarni](https://www.linkedin.com/in/subodh-kulkarni-21001611).

Rigetti currently makes processors on 150-millimeter wafers in its manual fab in Fremont, Calif. Kulkarni puts its yield near 50 percent, which he says is “good enough” for R&D when specs are changing frequently. But Anderon promises more reliable automated chip production that companies like Rigetti could retain to advance their own chip development. “We find that to be very attractive,” Kulkarni says, “not because of capacity, but because of capability.”

Like conventional silicon foundries, Anderon plans to offer process design kits, or PDKs, specifying the rules designers must follow to use its manufacturing processes. “They design, we build,” Khare says. Customization will also be available, he adds, and the foundry will protect clients’ intellectual property and operate neutrally, including for IBM’s competitors.

Making that model work will require predictable fabrication. For superconducting qubits, a critical component is the Josephson junction, which consists of two superconductors separated by a thin insulating barrier. Variations in junction area and barrier thickness can change critical current and qubit frequency, potentially creating unwanted frequency overlaps and reducing chip yield.

Anderon’s automated line could help control variation through repeatable patterning, deposition, and oxidation, with in-line testing to identify process drift. But customers will need to measure the actual improvement in qubit performance, Kulkarni says.

Anderon’s latest-generation 300mm quantum wafers.Anderon

Much of the fabrication equipment overlaps with that used for silicon chips, although superconducting circuits require specialized materials and process steps. Anderon [advertises](https://www.anderon.com/) superconducting qubit arrays, microwave components, and through-silicon connections. But extending manufacturing capabilities to other quantum technologies, like trapped ion or photonic qubits, would require additional process development that Anderon has not publicly detailed yet.

Semiconductor spin qubits can already be fabricated on conventional chip production lines, says [Lieven Vandersypen](https://qutech.nl/person/lieven-vandersypen/) of Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, while superconducting qubits need specialized steps that may require new development.

A dedicated quantum facility could spread costs and support the development of processes optimized for quantum devices, according to Vandersypen. “Understanding how to make this transition is timely and important,” he says.

Manufacturing capabilities alone will not make Anderon into quantum computing’s TSMC. It also needs sustained demand beyond IBM. Designers have alternatives. Vandersypen points to QuantWare’s investment in its own wafer-scale facility and Belgium’s Imec, which supplies prototype quantum chips rather than pursuing high-volume manufacturing. “Time will tell which model will prevail. Perhaps both will co-exist,” he says.

The Department of Commerce is backing several approaches to strengthen U.S. competitiveness in the global quantum market. While Anderon’s award is the largest so far, Commerce has finalized up to US $375 million for GlobalFoundries and up to $100 million each for Rigetti, D-Wave Quantum, Quantinuum, and PsiQuantum. [Those awards](https://spectrum.ieee.org/chips-act-impact-semiconductor-manufacturing) support manufacturing for multiple quantum architectures and address bottlenecks including readout electronics, cryostats, superconducting materials, optical components, and photonic packaging. Shared wafer fabrication is one piece of the larger engineering effort.

Khare says he can deliver wafers to outside customers by the end of the year. For potential customers such as Rigetti, the test will be how reliably those chips meet increasingly demanding designs. As Kulkarni puts it: “If we tighten the specification, what would the yield be?”

items.title: Engineering Multipole Resonances in Dielectric Metasurfaces for Transmission, Reflection, and Absorption Control
items.content:
Dielectric metasurfaces have moved to the forefront of nanophotonics, offering flat, low-loss alternatives to conventional bulk optical elements for controlling the amplitude, phase, and polarization of light. These structures are of growing interest to researchers and engineers working on sensing, energy harvesting, and flat optics, as their performance hinges on precisely engineered optical resonances. Full-wave finite element simulation, combined with semianalytical multipole decomposition in the COMSOL Multiphysics® software, gives us a way to not only predict these resonances but also uncover their underlying physical origins.

In this webinar, Dr. Pavel Terekhov, postdoctoral researcher at National Institute of Standards and Technology, will trace how a single quadrumer meta-atom, originally studied for its magnetic octupole response, evolves into two distinct light manipulation regimes. He will first revisit the foundational single-particle results that motivated this work, then show how arranging quadrumers into a periodic crystalline silicon metasurface produces anomalous absorption enhancement, governed by two independent multipole mechanisms coexisting in the same structure. Building on this, he will then introduce ongoing work on a gallium nitride metasurface, where the complex interplay of four different multipoles is used to sculpt reflection and transmission spectra including the quasi-bound-states-in-the-continuum (q-BIC) manipulation.

Attendees will see how COMSOL Multiphysics® and multipole decomposition connect full-wave simulation and analytical insight, turning abstract resonance behavior into physically interpretable design rules. The broader takeaway is that multipole-based simulation is not just a diagnostic tool but a design strategy: It enables the on-demand tailoring of absorption, reflection, and transmission in dielectric metasurfaces, with direct relevance to sensing, energy harvesting, and future optical device applications.

**Key Takeaways:**

- Learn about modeling multipole resonances in dielectric metasurfaces using full-wave finite element simulation and semianalytical multipole decomposition in COMSOL Multiphysics®.

- See how multipole-based simulation can be used to understand and control absorption, reflection, and transmission in silicon and gallium nitride metasurfaces.

- Explore how different multipole mechanisms, including quasi-bound states in the continuum (q-BICs), can be engineered to tailor optical responses for sensing, energy harvesting, and flat optics.

- Gain insights into how simulation and multipole decomposition can help researchers and engineers turn complex resonance behavior into practical design strategies for future optical devices.

items.title: Unveiling IC-STAR: Full-Flow Autonomy from Digital to Analog
items.content:
Learn how engineers can shift from manually managing tools and handoffs to defining objectives and supervising AI-driven execution across the silicon development lifecycle.

### Key Takeaways

- Explore four critical technologies enabling silicon design autonomy

- Understand how autonomous AI accelerates complex engineering workflows

- See real-world impact across semiconductor design and verification

- Gain practical insights from Ambiq’s deployment of autonomous AI in production
